name: CTCMath
line: CTCMath teaches by video lesson, then questions. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs CTCMath: CTCMath teaches by video lesson, then questions. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: CTCMath teaches by video lesson: a short tutorial, then questions, in the course order or the lessons an adult assigns [1][5]. Review comes in weekly sets in grades 1 to 8 [7]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. CTCMath's placement tests cover one K-8 topic at a time and list lessons that may need review [2]. Cathy Duffy notes that the program does not automatically prescribe a grade level or course from the tests [4]. The next lesson is the next one in the course, or one the adult assigns with a due date [5][6].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In CTCMath the unit is the lesson. It opens with a video tutorial of about 4 to 9 minutes, and the questions follow [1][4]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages. The data are correlational [11].

reasons.title: Typed answers, checked exactly
reasons.body: Many AMP problems need a typed number, a fraction, lines of work or a plotted point, not a choice. Every answer is checked exactly. Most CTCMath worksheets are multiple choice [2], and a review notes that students can sometimes work backward from the choices [5]. Some of its Algebra and Geometry lessons are graded by the student against worked solutions [2].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In CTCMath the parent sets the passing score and how many attempts come before worked solutions appear [6]. A student with a low score can rewatch the tutorial and try a new set [4].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. CTCMath's courses for grades 1 to 8 include Weekly Revision Tasks [5][7], and Cathy Duffy describes printable weekly review sheets [4]. We found none in its Kindergarten or high school courses [7]. Further review is a question set the adult builds by topic, difficulty and length [4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [10].

rows.range: Kindergarten through calculus, in courses: K-8, Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra II, Pre-Calculus with Trigonometry, and Calculus [2][3].
rows.start: Optional placement tests for each K-8 topic list lessons to review. They do not automatically prescribe a grade level or course [2][4].
rows.teaching: A video tutorial of about 4 to 9 minutes, then questions, with worked solutions after submitting [1].
rows.next: The course order, or lessons the adult assigns with due dates [5]. Reviewers say questions get easier or harder with performance [4][5].
rows.mastery: A passing score the parent sets, and a number of attempts before solutions appear [6].
rows.review: Weekly Revision Tasks in grades 1 to 8, and question sets the adult builds by topic, difficulty and length [4][7].
rows.print: A one-page summary with each tutorial, worked solutions, weekly review sheets, and worksheets built by topic, difficulty and length [1][4].
rows.adult: Can assign lessons and due dates, set the passing score and attempts, and build extra question sets [4][5][6].
rows.reports: Every lesson attempt with pass or fail, score and time, and a weekly emailed report [1][2].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on the pages we read. No entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse when we checked [8][9].

theirs: CTCMath is an online math course for kindergarten through grade 12. Cathy Duffy's review says Australian math teacher Patrick Murray created it and teaches it [4]. Its courses run from K-8 through Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra II, Pre-Calculus with Trigonometry, and Calculus [3].

A lesson starts with a tutorial of about 4 to 9 minutes, narrated over animation. Then the learner answers questions, marked automatically with worked solutions after submitting, or works a printable worksheet [1]. A one-page summary prints with each tutorial [1]. Placement tests for each K-8 topic list lessons that may need review [2], the adult can assign lessons with due dates [5], and grades 1 to 8 include Weekly Revision Tasks [7].
credit: A short video lesson for each topic from one teacher, with a printable summary [1][4].
A weekly review habit built into grades 1 to 8 [4][7].

theirs: We found no outcome study of CTCMath on the pages of its site we read [1][3]. It had no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse when we checked [8][9].
ours: The two findings that bear on this comparison: mixed and spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, on the researchers' own test, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [10]; and in an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages, in data the authors call correlational [11]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child likes to watch a teacher explain a topic before trying it.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want typed answers checked exactly, and help that never counts as learned.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, mixed with other math.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from CTCMath?
questions.answer: CTCMath teaches by video lesson, then questions, in the course order or the lessons an adult assigns [1][5]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does CTCMath work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of CTCMath on the pages of its site we read [1][3]. It had no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse when we checked [8][9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
